data.title: Celtic hillforts in present-day Slovakia as centres of craft production
data.excerpt: The Celts played a significant role in the historical development of Europe, and the many excavations and finds across the continent enrich the study of their past. This study presents their hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia as centres of craft production – iron smelting and smithing, jewellery making, pottery and stone working.

timeline.title: The Celtic people north of the Alps
timeline.description: In the middle of the last millennium BC the community of the Celts came into being north-west of the Alps through a complex process, and they soon spread their name across the whole of Europe as it then was.

timeline.title: The La Tène period
timeline.description: The period of the greatest flowering of Celtic culture in Europe, named after the site of La Tène by Lake Neuchâtel; it is a culture of the Late Iron Age.

timeline.title: Celtic incursions into the Carpathian Basin
timeline.description: The Celts were among the greatest barbarian peoples of the world of that time and their expansion reached the Carpathian Basin as well.

timeline.title: The arrival of the Celts in the territory of present-day Slovakia
timeline.description: During their eastern campaign the Celts penetrated the Carpathian Basin, where they met the long-settled population of the Vekerzug group and the surviving Hallstatt occupation.

timeline.title: The emergence of the Púchov culture
timeline.description: The movement of Germanic tribes caused the Celtic population to resettle from the Danubian lowlands into the mountainous areas of central and northern Slovakia, and so the Púchov culture came into being.

timeline.title: The peak of the Púchov culture
timeline.description: The resettlement into northern Slovakia culminated and the Púchov culture reached its maximum territorial extent, from the Spiš region to north-eastern Moravia and southern Poland.

timeline.year: the beginning of the Roman period
timeline.title: Economic decline
timeline.description: At the turn of the Late La Tène and the Roman period economic and civilisational decline set in, although the craft tradition was partly preserved in the area of the Strečno gorge and at settlements in northern Slovakia.

children.text: The Celts played a significant role in the historical development of Europe. The large number of excavations and finds made so far at various sites in Europe contribute to enriching the study of the Celtic past. They are evidence of the crystallisation, expansion and artistic activity in this extensive geographical area. As Lamiová puts it: “We know little about the origins of the Celts.” (Lamiová, 1982, p. 11). The time to which we can place the beginnings of Celtic history reaches back to the start of the 2nd millennium BC. The Celtic people appear in the territory north of the Alps in the middle of the last millennium BC, that is, in the 5th century BC. North-west of the Alps the community of this remarkable people was born through a complex process; being the first of the barbarian peoples, as the southern world called them, they became the classic representative of the barbarian world. The Celts held a prominent position among the barbarians. The term “Celt” was first used by Herodotus, but his knowledge of this people is limited and rather inaccurate. From Caesar's time to the present day the Celts have been described as the inhabitants of the territory between the Rhine, the Alps, the Mediterranean Sea, the Pyrenees and the Atlantic Ocean. Certain indications of a Celtic presence are also found on the Iberian Peninsula. The culture of the Celts at the time of their greatest flowering in Europe (5th – 1st century BC) is named after La Tène, the Swiss site by Lake Neuchâtel, as the La Tène culture (and period), a culture of the Late Iron Age, which followed the culture of the Early Iron Age known as the Hallstatt. From the 5th century BC the name of the Celts spread rapidly across Europe as it then was. In the western coastal part of France and England the Celts were the builders of megalithic monuments erected from large blocks of stone: on the one hand menhirs (tall upright monoliths) and dolmens (burial chambers made of large boulders), on the other long stone or circular structures (Stonehenge).

In the 4th century BC the Celts were among the greatest barbarian peoples of the world of that time. And yet this people never created an ethnic unity, nor a unified state formation, an empire that would have united the most varied tribal units. They were fragmented into a multitude of larger and smaller tribal formations that spoke different dialects. The Celtic impact, which we record in extensive areas from Ireland and Great Britain across the whole of Europe as far as the Balkan Peninsula and into Asia Minor, was not only military and destructive. It also brought with it new creative insights. Celtic civilisation, however, was characterised not only by the way it buried its dead, but also by its material culture. Well-armed groups of the Celtic people took a significant part in the settlement of northern Europe and also attacked, harshly and without hesitation, the most important centres of the educated south; they struck at northern Italy, indeed at Rome itself, penetrated as far as Sicily, while other streams moved into the Carpathian Basin, the Balkans and even Asia Minor. Archaeological finds show that at the turn of the 5th and 4th centuries BC the Celts turned their attention to the centres in the Danube region. “In the course of the 4th century the Carpathian Basin too felt the Celtic incursions.” (Filip, 1995, p. 65). The Celts penetrated the Carpathian Basin, and thus also the territory of present-day Slovakia, during their eastern campaign around 300 BC, where they met the long-settled population of the Vekerzug group and the surviving occupation in the north and east that still dated from the preceding Hallstatt period. They lived with it in symbiosis. Since in the Tisza region the Celts came up against the Scythian barrier, they had to turn to the south-east, towards the Balkan Peninsula. The significance of the expeditions into the Carpathian Basin, as Filip notes, lay in: “contact with the local cultures, not only with the Scythian but also with the native Illyrian and Thraco-Dacian culture, and also contact with the Greek world of the time.” (Filip, 1995, p. 65). This was reflected not only in the military and economic sphere, but above all in the artistic one. At the time of their greatest expansion, that is in the 4th century BC, the Celts occupied almost the whole of Europe. Their presence is evident in Gaul and Germania. We detect their influence on the southern borders of Poland, in Hungary, Transylvania, Italy, Iberia and Great Britain. In ancient times part of Bohemia and Moravia also belonged to the original Celtic territory, and in later centuries new streams of Celts came to control a considerable part of present-day Slovakia, which lies in the northern part of the Middle Danube region and whose fertile lowlands and mineral wealth attracted various ethnic groups, above all the Celts and the Germanic peoples. The expansion of the Celts did not mean the occupation of the whole territory of present-day Slovakia. They settled the less fertile northern areas to a lesser extent; their aim was to settle the fertile eastern areas, but also the most fertile areas lying in the south and south-west. The presence of this ethnic group in the territory of present-day Slovakia is also attested by Celtic cemeteries and find spots. Since this country lay on the edge of Celtic interests, the first Celtic contact here was not extensive, as is shown by the fact that the finds from this territory are not very numerous or rich. The occupation of this territory proceeded in a logical historical continuity. “First it was only influence and imitation, later military expansion and finally the permanent settlement of the territory of present-day Slovakia by Celtic tribes.” (Furmánek et al., 1991, p. 60). The Celtic expansion first affected the south-western part of Slovakia. Since the penetration of the Celts into this territory was at first infrequent, the first wave of Celtic expansion did not directly affect the areas lying further north. Because of the great geographical diversity of the territory of Slovakia and the impact of foreign cultures, cultural groups and ethnic groups in the La Tène period, the occupation had a differing character. In the territory of present-day Slovakia we distinguish three areas of occupation in the La Tène period. The first area of occupation is the territory of western Slovakia; the second area can be identified as central and northern Slovakia, which is characterised by the Púchov culture; and finally there is the territory of eastern Slovakia. The gradual crystallisation of the La Tène period in Slovakia, whose division follows Reinecke's division into the Early, Older, Middle and Late La Tène period, was influenced by the results of excavations at many fortified settlements or hillforts, which from a functional point of view are regarded as the predecessors of the later medieval castles and which we also encounter in this territory.

blocks.alt: CELTIC HILLFORTS IN THE TERRITORY OF PRESENT-DAY SLOVAKIA AS CENTRES OF CRAFT PRODUCTION

children.text: The focus of my work is the question of Celtic strongpoints – hillforts, which I attempt to present above all as centres of artistic and craft activities. These played an important role in every strongpoint of the hillfort type, the result of the activities mentioned being not only to cover the needs of the occupants of the given hillfort, but also to secure a certain surplus, which became the object of trade exchanges. We learn about the economic development of the Celts in the territory of present-day Slovakia mainly from settlement finds, especially from the oppidum environment and from the Púchov culture. The economic potential of individual settlements depended on several factors, above all on their position and natural conditions. The prestige of a settlement rose with its strategically significant position. Many of them arose in the positions most advantageous for communication, but also on the sites of older settlements along a river or in the vicinity of raw-material sources, for example the iron ores in the area of the Lesser Carpathians, whose extraction is undoubtedly connected with smithing or with the production of coins. The causes of the demise of old centres of craft production – Celtic hillforts – and of the emergence of new ones are considered to be not only economic reasons connected with the strategic position of individual hillforts, but above all the power-political consequences connected with the ethnic movements that took place at the end of the 2nd century BC. From ancient accounts we learn of the movement of Germanic tribes from north to south as a result of climatic changes, which influenced the settlement structure in the area of the Carpathians; as a consequence the population concentrated in the mountain areas, and with this is undoubtedly connected the emergence of the Púchov culture and of new oppida in the Danube region at the end of the Middle and the beginning of the Late La Tène period. Apart from the features the oppida had in common, topographical and chronological differences can be observed between them. The first difference lies in the placing of production hamlets in the vicinity of the hillforts, which was characteristic of the oppida of the eastern part of the Danube region. “This model was applied, with variations, not only in the mixed Celtic-Dacian area of Pannonia, south-western Slovakia and the northern Tisza region, but also in the Púchov culture in the mountain area of the Carpathians” (Pieta, 2008, p. 43). The chronological difference is connected with the production and trading opportunities that had a marked share in the demise of some centres as early as around the last century BC, while others survived into the Roman period thanks to contacts with the surrounding world, as is attested by finds of coins and other imports in the territory of present-day Slovakia, for example at the oppidum at
Trenčianske Bohuslavice
and at the settlements of
Šaštín-Stráže,
Chorvátsky Grob and Slovenský Grob

, coming from the Mediterranean, the northern Balkans and also from neighbouring Pannonia and Noricum. In some cases we encounter the names of individual sites several times, because many of them were used in an earlier period as well – already in later prehistory and in the Roman period – and even survived into the Middle Ages, which is due above all to the naturally advantageous strategic position of these hillforts, which often survived until the medieval period. The Celtic hillforts of western Slovakia were spread over two different regions, one of which is the adjacent Danube region in south-western Slovakia with several production centres, of which the best known are the lowland Middle La Tène settlement at
Šaštín-Stráže
in the Záhorie Lowland, where coin minting is attested, and the Late La Tène hillforts such as the Bratislava oppidum, the site of
Bratislava – Devín
and the small settlement of
Nitriansky Hrádok
. The centre of
Komárno
also had a craft character, as six pottery kilns demonstrate. The second region comprises the northern mountainous part, from which we may also mention the Hallstatt centre at
Smolenice
, and later the Early La Tène fortified seat on
Slepý vrch at Horné Orešany
, focused on smithing. From the end of the Middle La Tène period comes the hillfort of
Plavecké Podhradie – Pohanská,

perhaps the best known in this region, whose material culture can be characterised through craft activity and its two components: iron products and pottery. Craft activity here is attested by a quantity of iron objects coming either directly from the acropolis or from the area outside it. The iron inventory is represented by tools (small axes, knives, spring shears, small saws, drills, chisels, various cramps, clamps, cramp-clamps – half-clamps, nails, hooks, sheet-metal fittings), by metal components of wooden implements (a fragment of a handle and fragments of two attachment loops – attachments – from a wooden bucket), by weapons and by jewellery (brooches). The ceramic material from this site is distinguished by great variety. A distinctive component of the pottery products at Pohanská consists of graphite pottery and the production of graphite vessels, on the bases of which potter's marks occurred. Stamped pottery is poorly represented, since stamping in the decoration of vessel surfaces is a typical procedure in the ornamentation of Middle La Tène products. Of painted pottery, only a single painted vessel, found in fragments, is mentioned. Of the stone industry, the most frequent finds are stone crushers, whetstones of various shapes and querns, whose production at Pohanská is demonstrated by a stone-carving and sculpture workshop. According to the archaeological reports, however, most similar material was imported into this area. Craft production was also recorded in the second area, which comprises the mountainous, rugged
part of central and northern Slovakia
, characterised by the
Púchov culture
, whose beginnings are connected with the resettlement of the Celtic population from the Danubian lowlands into its mountainous areas as a
consequence of the invasion of the Germanic Cimbri

in this period. As Pieta adds: “In the second half of the 2nd century we already reckon with a Celtic presence in the mountain areas of Slovakia, north-eastern Moravia and southern Poland, which we regard as the characteristic and the time of the emergence of the Púchov culture.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 55).

blocks.alt: CELTIC HILLFORTS IN THE TERRITORY OF PRESENT-DAY SLOVAKIA AS CENTRES OF CRAFT PRODUCTION

children.text: The process of resettlement into northern Slovakia culminated in the Late La Tène period, when the
Púchov culture
reached its maximum territorial extent. “

Its territory extended from the eastern border of the Spiš region in the east to north-eastern Moravia in the west and the spurs of the Carpathians and the Beskids in southern Poland, as far as the Žarnovica – Trenčín line in the south

.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 57). It manifested itself most markedly in the north of the territory of Slovakia. Because of better trading contacts with the surrounding world and openness to western and southern imports, the Púchov culture manifested itself less markedly in the west of this territory. This fact was reflected in the minting of coins inspired by the Bohemian or Pannonian milieu. Brooches of composite construction with a long spring are also represented here. In central Slovakia its distribution is the least well known. On the basis of archaeological excavations at settlements in central Slovakia, Celtic craft activity in the Early La Tène period cannot be adequately demonstrated. From the Older La Tène period we know only bronze brooches from
Sebeslavce near Martin
. The Middle La Tène period we designate as the pre-Púchov horizon, which reached into the Liptov area. The existence of the Púchov culture we detect
only in the Late La Tène period
. Products from the settlements in the upper Nitra region (
Krnča, Malé Kršteňany, Hradec near Prievidza
) have a Púchov character, as do those from the best-known Púchov settlement, the fortified hilltop settlement on the hill
Havránok in the Liptov region
near Liptovská Mara, and in the Orava region (
Trniny above Veľký Bysterec

Even though at the turn of the end of the Late La Tène period and the beginning of the Roman period we record an economic and civilisational decline whose consequences were reflected in the material culture, the continuity of occupation was preserved in part of the Púchov territory, as was the tradition of craft production in the area of the Strečno gorge and at several settlements in northern Slovakia. Craft production in the east of the country is demonstrated by finds recorded from several Late La Tène settlements, of which the best known is the fortified settlement at
Zemplín

situated in the southern part of the East Slovak Lowland. Various kinds of production activity were concentrated in smaller settlement units in the immediate vicinity of the hillfort, as the pottery kiln found there proves. Since besides the Celts the Dacians too were interested in settling in this territory in this period, the production of goods has a culturally mixed Celtic-Dacian character, of which we are persuaded by the ceramic inventory, represented not only by Celtic wheel-thrown pottery and the situla-shaped pots and large storage vessels present, but also by Dacian pottery in the form of footed bowls, conical handled cups and coarse utility ware. The metal inventory also has a Late La Tène character, represented above all by iron brooches, iron and bronze spurs, working tools and fittings. The basis of the rich Celtic material culture is the development of craft.

The material culture of La Tène civilisation can be characterised through craft activity and its components – the production of pottery, the working of iron, jewellery making and stone working. The technique of pottery production also spread into non-Celtic areas, either through trade or through efforts at local imitation. The Celts certainly brought pottery making, one of the oldest craft activities, to a higher level than had been the case in the preceding period, as is demonstrated by the
invention of the fast-rotating potter's wheel

, which contributed to the production of often perfectly symmetrical vessels, of large dimensions and with a rich range of forms. Decorative and ornamental elements were an inseparable part of the pottery produced. Ornament played an essential role in Celtic art. The motifs were drawn directly from nature and from the imitation of the rhythms of the working process, but cult and religious ideas were also reflected in them. Among the Celts in particular, craft activity was conditioned by the basic craft, iron smelting, or rather smithing, which is represented by iron products and high-quality weapons. The quantity of iron products and production waste at the settlements only confirms the importance and significance of the extraction and working of this metal, the result of which was economic development, progress and a high technical level in the individual craft activities, in agriculture, building, transport and the warfare of the time. Heaps of production waste are found at the well-known metallurgical centre of
Varín
in the Žilina district, at
Nový Smokovec
or
Veľký Slavkov
in the sub-Tatra area, at the settlements of the Púchov culture at the settlement of Liptovská Mara IV and at
Likavka

in the area of the Choč mountains in the Liptov region, and in the extensive iron-ore region on the southern Slovak–Hungarian border, which, like most settlements in this territory, has been little explored. With the development of the basic Celtic craft – iron smelting – the social standing of smiths and metallurgists also rose extraordinarily; they play an important role in mythology as well, as Pieta adds: “Work with metal and fire has from ancient times had a special significance, not only for the creation of undoubtedly significant real values, but also for its mystical dimension, manifested in the social standing of these craftsmen.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 142). That the foundations of the production of iron objects in this territory were laid by the Celtic population is attested by the account of the Roman historian Tacitus, who mentions the Celtic tribe of the Cotini as producers of iron, and by the account of Claudius Ptolemy, who in this connection mentions the Quadi. Craft activity is brought closer to us by the rich grave and settlement finds from south-western and eastern Slovakia documented by archaeological excavations, but also by oppidum finds and hoards of tools and implements from Púchov centres such as
Plavecké Podhradie, Trenčianske Bohuslavice, Slatina nad Bebravou, Liptovská Mara and Folkušová

. “Craft work with iron is usually attested only by production waste – slag, hammerscale and fragments of products or semi-finished products of this metal.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 145). In this territory we have several areas concerned with the production of iron metals and alloys and their further working at that time. In western Slovakia it is the Lesser Carpathian area and the production centres of
Studienka
and Plavecké Podhradie from the end of the Middle La Tène period. Metallurgical activity was also recorded at
Spišské Tomášovce
– Čingov in the Spiš region and around
Hrabušice
in the area of the northern foothills of the Slovak Paradise.

There are various methods of working, shaping and joining metals, which is influenced by their properties and by the temperature of heating achieved, while the process of heating forms the main part of the smith's craft skill. In this section we shall look more closely at some of the main procedures important in the treatment of metals. The shaping and joining of an iron object is achieved by several technical operations. In shaping an object this involves cutting, upsetting, twisting, splitting and punching, while in joining, welding, riveting or hot pinning is used. One of the basic ways of shaping metals and forming their dimensions is
forging

, by which the properties of the material used can be changed on the one hand, and on the other the material can be freed of impurities and various admixtures by this process, so that – as with further heat treatment of the product once the desired shape has been achieved – a higher quality is attained. The oldest way of hardening steel material, which is done by rapidly cooling the heated object in cold, salt or oily water or in oil, is called quenching. Its opposite is
tempering

, the aim of which is to reduce the brittleness of the hardened iron, thereby increasing its toughness. Improvement of the product is also achieved by various ways of treating its surface. One of these ways is carburising, that is, the addition of carbon to the surface of the object or its hardening, while the core remains softer and therefore more flexible. Further surface treatments and at the same time the final operations in the production of an object include
filing
, subsequent smoothing or
polishing

with the aid of special tools such as files, grinding stones or polishing compounds. Even though the architectural characteristics of Iron Age smithies are unknown, we do know that their basic components were a hearth, bellows for raising the heat by means of a stream of air, a working base –
an anvil

, a vessel for cooling the metal, and a set of tools and implements needed for carrying out the metalworking craft, whether that of the smith or of the sheet-metal worker. Master smiths used a wide range of metalworking implements, which was reflected in the quality of their products. That in their work they handled hammers, anvils, tongs, cutters, dishing tools, punches, files and forge shovels is attested by hoards of iron objects at settlements or in the graves of craftsmen.
The basic working tools, made of well-hardened material, were
hammers,
which occur sporadically as early as the Hallstatt period, as is attested by the finds from below the hillfort of
Klapy near Udiča
, which we date to a period somewhere between the Hallstatt and the Middle La Tène period. Further finds come from the
Čertova džura
cave near Spišské Tomášovce, from the early Celtic hillfort at Horné Orešany, from Plavecké Podhradie and from the Púchov area, which in this connection is represented by the site of
Skalka nad Váhom
, the settlement of Liptovská Mara III and Spišské Tomášovce – Čingov. A double-ended hammer was found at the hillfort of
Slatina nad Bebravou
. Exceptional finds include
iron anvils

used as a base for finer specialised sheet-metalworking or jewellery work, found at Plavecké Podhradie, Slatina nad Bebravou, Folkušová and at the settlement of Liptovská Mara III. Another basic smith's tool was the
forge shovel

, needed when working with embers or charcoal. Pieta describes what the forge shovels looked like as follows: “Some had a wooden shaft, but in most cases they were large all-metal implements with a long, often twisted handle ending in a flat plate with a spherical terminal or in an eye with a suspension ring.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 147). The oldest forge shovel comes from a woman's grave at Palárikovo, further pieces from the hillfort of Udrina near Slatina nad Bebravou, from Plavecké Podhradie, Liptovská Mara II, Folkušová and Trenčianske Bohuslavice, and such an implement is presumed from the hillfort of Bratislava – Devín. For gripping heated pieces of metal, holding casting crucibles, and assembling and shaping products, jointed or lever
tongs
served, consisting of two arms passing into jaws loosely joined by a pin; they gradually became specialised and have essentially not changed since the Iron Age. The oldest find comes from
Udiča
and further numerous finds are from Plavecké Podhradie and Folkušová. For more detailed shaping and coarser surface treatment,
files

of especially hard steel were used. Both settlement finds and the graves of craftsmen are poor in this valuable tool. Finds of files have been recorded at Horné Orešany, Chotín, Trenčianske Bohuslavice, Slatina nad Bebravou and Varín. The occurrence of iron semi-finished products is attested as early as the Hallstatt period in the form of loaves, such as were used above all in the local milieu. As Pieta adds: “They were the resulting product of the working of the iron sponge obtained by smelting the ore.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 149). They were found at Liptovská Mara, Horné Orešany, Plavecké Podhradie and in part at settlements and sites of the Púchov culture in western Slovakia. The technical level of the producers is demonstrated by various tools and implements, but we are best convinced of it on the basis of the production of
knives

, whose beginnings reach back to the Upper Palaeolithic, when they took the form of blades. Knives belonged to the universal working implements and occasional weapons whose size, shape and form was adapted to needs, whether for kitchen, table and ritual use, or they were used in surgery and in hygiene or in the more demanding working of organic materials, especially wood and leather. Given the large number of knives of various sizes and shapes, it was necessary to classify them for the sake of better characterisation. Such a classification of knives is offered by Pieta in his work Keltské osídlenie Slovenska (The Celtic Occupation of Slovakia). “They can be classified according to the size and shape of the blade or the edge (cleaver-like, curved, sickle-shaped, straight, special), or according to the shape or treatment of the handle (ring terminals, tang terminals, grips with riveted plating).” (Pieta, 2008, p. 149). Heavy knives – cleavers – are typical of warrior graves from the Late Hallstatt period onwards. The finds from this territory come from the settlement of Liptovská Mara III and from the sites of Kremnička, Čachtice and Poniky. We also encounter them on the eastern periphery of the Celtic world.

For the southern areas, such as the Balkans, knives – daggers with a narrower blade curved forward and a handle fastened with one or more rivets – are typical. From this territory, finds are attested from the settlement of Liptovská Mara II, Plavecké Podhradie, Trenčianske Bohuslavice, Jasenica and Folkušová. Of all the types, the most widespread were the large knives belonging to the bearers of the Przeworsk culture, which were distributed as far as the borders of the Mediterranean, with the exception of eastern Slovakia, where these knives are absent. Pieta describes them as follows: “The most widespread were large knives with a characteristic ring handle and a blade with a slightly curved back and a more or less straight or slightly curved edge.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 153).
The smithing production of the Púchov culture, or of the Late La Tène period, was of excellent standard

, as is attested by the objects from Liptovská Mara. The production of knives in the Celtic world was influenced by the classical milieu, but also by foreign, non-Celtic influences and models.
 
 Even though iron held a dominant position in craft activity, bronze and silver also retained their significance for their decorative quality and good utility properties in the production of ornamental objects and embellishments, which were the product of jewellers.
Jewellers

made ornaments of bronze and silver, while also using valuable foreign materials such as coral or amber. Typical products were wire bracelets, torcs, finger rings and chains. Silver products are not typical of the Carpathian area. An exception, however, is the find from Kostoľany pod Tribečom, where an Eneolithic hoard with copper, silver and gold objects was discovered. In Slovakia, metalworking or jewellery production has not been subjected to systematic archaeological research. Evidence of metal production is attested from only a few sites in this territory, namely from Nitra – Párovské Háje, Lipová – Ondrochov, Chotín, Trenčianske Bohuslavice, Bratislava – Staré Mesto and Devín, and from the territory of the Púchov culture the centres of Folkušová or Jánovce – Machalovce and the settlement of Liptovská Mara III. Smaller production centres include Kežmarok and Kvačany. Celtic craftsmen attained real mastery in casting, which represented the basic working procedure in the treatment of non-ferrous and precious metals. The essence of this production technique lay in the melting of metal heated in melting crucibles placed in small furnaces over charcoal or directly in the embers, where the flame was supplied with oxygen by blowing with bellows, so that a very high temperature was reached which made it possible to cast the molten metal into moulds.
The casting procedure
was described to us by Pieta as follows:

“Metal melted sufficiently (to a bright glow) was cast into simple loaf-shaped casting lumps or rod-shaped bars. In the making of often technically complex utility objects and jewellery it was filled into moulds either by simply pouring the metal into the neck of the mould, or (in the case of demanding products or serial tree-casting) by making use of centrifugal force with a sling (Schleuderguss).

” (Pieta, 2008, p. 156). As proof that this working procedure was also carried out at the oppida and lowland settlements of this territory, we have the archaeological evidence of the remains of small furnaces, plates for casting coin blanks, technical ceramics of various shapes, metal casting lumps, one- or two-part casting moulds and fragments of used crucibles. In Slovakia there are places where traces of casting have been found. Casting plates were found at Bratislava, Šaštín and Liptovská Mara. Casting moulds come from Devín, Trenčianske Bohuslavice, Chorvátsky Grob and Jánovce – Machalovce. Relatively well known from Slovak settlements are
casting moulds

of fine-grained sandstone, more rarely of clay; the prevailing forms, however, are medium-sized crucibles of conical shape with a pointed base, while bowl-shaped, bucket-shaped and barrel-shaped forms of various sizes are rarer. Finely levigated or graphite clay was most often used for their production. From the territory of the Púchov culture we know melting crucibles found at Liptovská Mara, Kežmarok, Kvačany and Púchov. Further evidence of casting is provided by the objects themselves, which have survived from the time of the Celtic occupation of Slovakia. As Pieta adds: “Particularly admirable works are
pseudo-filigree jewellery, basket-shaped bronze pendants, belt clasps, strap ends, rings and small rings with plastic decoration, and also the guide rings of horse harness
and other demanding metal-casting works, generally made in a lost mould.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 156). Among the objects listed,
gold earrings

from Divinka and Dolný Kubín – Veľký Bysterec are also represented. Brooches also appear. Besides casting we also encounter other metalworking techniques, of which the most common and technically least demanding was hammering and shaping, used above all in work with small objects, which often served as a decorative component of clothing. Sheet-metal products, which in the Older and Middle La Tène period appeared only rarely compared with the late period, when they came to the fore, were the result of repoussé work. Bronze and iron were worked by this technique, and from them not only components of utility objects and vessels were made, but also the ornamental mountings of buckets, caskets, wagons and other wooden artefacts, and further of belts, various appliqués and horse harness. An exceptional goldsmith's technique is joining, which was done in several ways, for example by riveting or by suspension. It was used for joining the individual parts of an object, especially of precious metal.

Although stone is the oldest raw material needed for making objects, its use by humans in the Iron Age narrowed to the construction of the various types of fortification systems. The most significant stone product, which marked the overall economic and technological progress of the Early Historical period, was the invention of the rotary
stone quern

with an adjustable fineness of grinding, coarse milling or dehusking, which came here from the Mediterranean area. Its development is not known in detail. “It is presumed that the first step towards the use of mechanical motion in grinding grain was the principle of the so-called Greek mill.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 161). Finds of this kind in the Middle Danube region are rare and appear only exceptionally at the sites of Liptovská Mara and Žilina – Strážov. The properties of a quern were influenced by the material used in its production. The first querns in this territory were made of Tatra crystalline granite, but the most advantageous were porous volcanic rocks, especially the central Slovak rhyolites, for their hardness and structure. Their production and domestic use in the Danubian, Tisza and Carpathian areas of Slovakia, as Pieta informs us, ends at the beginning of the Roman period. To this day,
whetstones

are used in the production process or in sharpening implements. Once, carried on the belt together with a knife or a sword, they belonged to the basic male equipment, because they served for maintenance, mainly for sharpening tools and weapons. A division of abrasive artefacts from a functional point of view is offered by Pieta: “From a functional point of view we can divide abrasive artefacts into stationary ones (bases), over which the product is moved, and mobile ones – whetstones, with which the object is worked” (Pieta, 2008, p. 163). It should be added that after pottery, grinding stones are among the most frequent finds at settlements. Other stone objects whose purpose is unclear include stone slabs made of bedded sandstone. Pieta describes the procedure for making them as follows: “The individual slabs were roughly cut with a hammer or chisel into a polygon and their circumference was gradually rounded by further cutting, sometimes also by grinding.” (Pieta, 2008, p. 163). All these results of Celtic working activity mentioned in this article, entitled Hradiská Keltov na území Slovenska ako centrá remeselnej výroby (Celtic hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia as centres of craft production), are not only an attempt to assess the relationship between the kind of craft or craft activity and the space in this territory where this activity was carried out, but also an attempt to convey the contribution of the Celts in the field of craft production, which undoubtedly lies in its development, through many technical improvements and inventions.
